name: Time of supply — goods
definition: The time of supply of goods is the date fixed by s.12 at which the liability to pay tax on goods arises. Under forward charge it is the earlier of the date in s.12(2)(a) — the date of issue of invoice, or the last date on which the supplier was required under s.31 to issue it — and the date in s.12(2)(b), the date on which the supplier receives payment. Under reverse charge it is the earliest of receipt of goods, the date of payment in the recipient's records, and the date immediately following thirty days from the date of issue of invoice. Vouchers, residual cases and additions to value have their own sub-sections.
why_it_exists: It fixes WHEN the GST liability arises, and therefore which return period the entry belongs to. s.12(1) ties the liability itself to this date, so choosing the wrong date does not merely misdate an entry — it puts the tax in the wrong period. This is NOT the accounting revenue recognition date: GST time of supply and AS-9 revenue recognition are separate determinations and can land in different periods.
inputs: whether tax is payable on forward charge or reverse charge
the date of issue of invoice, and the last date on which s.31 required it to be issued
the date the supplier received payment — book entry date and bank credit date
for reverse charge: the date of receipt of goods, the recipient's book entry date and bank debit date
whether the supply is of vouchers, and whether the underlying supply is identifiable at issue
any addition to value by way of interest, late fee or penalty, and the date it was received
outputs: a single date — the time of supply of the goods
a separate date for any addition to value under s.12(6)
or an escalation, where a limb cannot be evaluated on the evidence held
preconditions: the transaction is a supply under s.7 (GST-SUPPLY-SCOPE)
it is classified as a supply of GOODS — if it is a supply of services, s.13 governs instead
there is NO change in the rate of tax — s.14 displaces s.12 if there is (GST-TIME-RATE-CHANGE-001)
exceptions: a change in the rate of tax — s.14 applies notwithstanding s.12 (GST-TIME-RATE-CHANGE-001)
excess received up to one thousand rupees — s.12(2) proviso, at the supplier's option (GST-TIME-GOODS-004)
additions to value by interest, late fee or penalty — s.12(6) (GST-TIME-GOODS-009)

common_mistakes: using the invoice date when payment was received first — s.12(2) says EARLIER, not the invoice
letting a late invoice postpone the tax point — s.12(2)(a) names the last date the supplier was REQUIRED to issue it
using the bank credit date when the payment was entered in the books earlier — Explanation 2 takes the earlier of the two
applying the SIXTY-day reverse-charge clock from s.13(3) to goods — s.12(3)(c) is THIRTY days
treating the time of supply as the accounting revenue recognition date — they are different determinations under different instruments and can fall in different periods
jumping to the residual rule in s.12(5) without first establishing that s.12(2), (3) and (4) genuinely could not be applied

CGST Act, 2017 s.14 — Change in rate of tax in respect of supply of goods or services

icai_references: NOT APPLICABLE — GST time of supply is a SEPARATE determination from accounting revenue recognition under AS-9. The two can fall in different periods and must never be conflated. ACC-REV-GOODS records the same boundary from the accounting side.
gst_references: CGST Act, 2017 s.12(1) to s.12(6), including the proviso to s.12(2), Explanations 1 and 2 to s.12(2), and the proviso to s.12(3)
evidence_required: the tax invoice, with its date of issue
proof of the date payment was received — the book entry and the bank credit
for reverse charge: proof of the date the goods were received, and the recipient's book entry and bank debit dates
for vouchers: whether the underlying supply was identifiable at issue
confidence_factors: weak when only the invoice is held — s.12(2)(b) needs the payment date, and the earlier of the two governs
weak when the s.31 due date for the invoice is unknown, because s.12(2)(a) can then only be evaluated on the actual issue date
weak when it is unclear whether the supply is on reverse charge — the whole sub-section changes
zero when a change in the rate of tax is in play — s.14 displaces this concept entirely and its limbs are not extracted
validation_checks: the chosen date is the EARLIEST of the applicable limbs, never a later one
the invoice date alone is never used where a payment date is available and earlier
the reverse-charge clock used is THIRTY days, not sixty
the time of supply is recorded separately from any accounting revenue recognition date, and the two are never reconciled by adjusting one to match the other
an addition to value under s.12(6) carries its own date and does not move the original supply
examples: invoice issued 10th, payment received 3rd, forward charge — time of supply is the 3rd, being the earlier of the two limbs of s.12(2)
reverse charge, goods received 5th, payment entered in the recipient's books 20th, invoice issued 1st — the thirty-day limb gives the 31st, so the earliest is the 5th
counterexamples: revenue recognised under AS-9 on transfer of risks and rewards on the 28th, with the invoice issued and payment received in the following month — the accounting date and the GST time of supply fall in different periods, and neither is evidence for the other
